USTR'S NEW TARIFF PROPOSALS. WHAT LIFESTYLE BRANDS NEED TO KNOW.

Your sourcing map just got redrawn, and the clock is already running.

Today the U.S. Trade Representative wrapped up its Section 301 investigations into "structural excess capacity" and found that the trade practices of 14 economies hurt U.S. commerce. 

It has now proposed new tariffs on all of them. 

None of this is final yet. 

But for anyone sourcing apparel, footwear or home goods overseas, this is the moment to start planning.

WHO GETS HIT HARDEST

Vietnam has the highest proposed rate, up to 35%, and textiles, apparel and footwear are named directly. India could see up to 25%, and China up to 20% on most goods. Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia are all looking at 18%, with Bangladesh's garment sector and Cambodia's and Indonesia's apparel industries called out by name. The EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland sit at 15%.

THE FINE PRINT MATTERS

These rates are ceilings. They're calculated net of existing tariffs, and every country has a list of exempt products. Several rates are also up for negotiation. Vietnam could drop to 20%, India to 17% and Singapore to 10% if they reach trade agreements. Your actual exposure depends on HTS codes, so look at the product annexes, not the headline numbers.

WHERE THERE'S NOWHERE TO HIDE

The usual escape routes are all on this list. Shifting production from China to Vietnam or Bangladesh doesn't save you much when every major Asian sourcing country is facing a similar rate. That changes the math on nearshoring, on dual sourcing, and on how much pricing power you really have.

THE TIMELINE

Written comments and requests to testify are due January 5, 2027. Public hearings start January 25. That means Fall 2027 costing is happening while the rules are still being written.

WHAT I'D DO THIS WEEK

Pull your landed cost by country and by HTS code. Model your margins at the proposed rates and at the negotiated rates. Talk to your factories about splitting costs, and figure out which SKUs can carry a price increase and which ones can't. 

If one of these tariffs would really hurt your business, think about filing a comment. 

The brands that model this now will have choices. 

The ones that wait will just have to react.

The Democratic Republic of #Congo is once again trying to raise#cobalt prices by banning exports. Just as in 2025, that may work for a few months, but could make the next cobalt price slump worse.

The problem is that banning exports does not necessarily stop cobalt from being mined. Much of Congo’s cobalt is produced as a by-product of copper. 

If production continues while exports stop, cobalt can pile up inside the country. That makes cobalt scarcer internationally today, while potentially pushing an even bigger surplus into tomorrow.

Congo is also no longer the only game in town.

#Indonesia had virtually no cobalt production capacity four years ago. Today it accounts for 16% of the global total, and my team at BloombergNEF expects that share to keep rising. 

Every intervention in Congo gives buyers another reason to diversify.

There is another escape route too: use less cobalt.#LFP batteries use none at all, while#NMC batteries are shifting toward lower-cobalt chemistries.

So Congo may succeed in lifting prices now. But the longer it holds material back, the more it risks encouraging alternative supply, substitution and a larger stockpile overhang later.

My team has looked at this in our new React, alongside the longer-term picture in the Transition Metals Outlook 2026. We also recently looked at the bigger question of what African countries need to turn their#CriticalMinerals resources into lasting economic value.

Links to all three are in the comments. If you’re not a#BNEF subscriber but would like to read them, let me know.

What gives first: Congo’s export controls, demand for cobalt, or prices?

Google just put a date on it. From January 2027, Android developer verification goes worldwide. Every app developer has to verify their identity with Google and register their apps, no matter where the app is distributed.
It started September 30 in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. In January it starts with seven stores: Google Play, Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo. Then it expands to every install source over a few months. Full enforcement is targeted for March 1, 2027.
Sideloading is not dead, but it gets painful. To install an app from an unverified developer you will have to open developer options, confirm nobody is pressuring you, restart your phone, wait 24 hours, then choose to allow it for 7 days or indefinitely. Google says the 24 hour wait is there to break phone scams that walk victims through an install in real time.
Google says millions of apps are already registered, over 99 percent of Android installs. The fight is about the rest: indie devs, open source apps, and APKs shared outside the stores.
If you build Android apps, register before January. If you install APKs from small devs, expect the extra steps soon.
What do you think, security win or the end of open Android?

We scored 10 markets across 12 product categories. The answer: start where Russian is spoken and returns are fastest.

3 hubs, in sequence:
1️⃣ Near abroad (fastest return)
Uzbekistan + Kazakhstan. 22.1% of Russian developers already sell in Kazakhstan — more than anywhere else. Belarus served by partner, no own hub. First offers: enterprise platforms, industrial/BIM, telecom billing, OS.
2️⃣ Gulf (big budgets, higher risk)
UAE as base → Saudi Arabia from it. MENA IT spend forecast at $169bn in 2026. No category scores above 55 — it's a budget market, not a fit market. Enter with near-abroad references.
3️⃣ Asia (largest long-term volume)
India ($24.7bn software spend) leads, but entry scores 2/5 — needs partners. Indonesia (~250M people) and Vietnam follow. One hub city chosen at G2.

Scores are judgment-based, not measured export data. Not legal advice.

The newly proposed Section 301 tariffs  (for “production overcapacity”) appear to not automatically stack on top of every Section 301 duty already in place. Take a Chinese-origin BESS DC container. USTR’s November 25 proposal would credit the existing 12.5% forced-labor tariff toward the proposed 20% rate. The separate 25% China battery tariff and 3.4% ordinary duty would still apply. That puts the total at 48.4%, up from 40.9% today. On a $1 million shipment, that’s $75,000 in additional duty. The main proposal would put Vietnam at 38.4%, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand at 21.4%, and South Korea, Japan and Taiwan at 15%. For developers pricing 2027 projects, these are scenarios for procurement budgets. The final rates will depend on trade talks: a qualifying U.S.–Vietnam agreement could bring Vietnam’s total down to 23.4%, while an unsatisfactory outcome with China could push its total as high as 68.4%.

🌾 Rice alternate wetting and drying
🐄 Livestock feed and manure management

When this happens, buyers can compare credits easily, and developers do not restart from zero in every country. Note that ACCF is an industry pact, so it doesn't bind any government yet.

Double Counting: When One Ton Is Sold Twice

Critiques of carbon projects in Indonesia have highlighted the persistent risk of double counting—occurring when projects are developed without government approval and overlap with national NDC accounting. In some cases, private-to-private offset trades have resulted in climate benefits being counted twice, because private sellers are not obligated to increase mitigation ambition as compensation for transferred offsets.

This is not a technical footnote. It strikes at the heart of carbon market credibility. If a single ton of emission reduction can be sold twice, then what the market is trading is not climate benefit—it is accounting fiction. And accounting fiction does not lower atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases.

The integrity of verification systems depends entirely on their ability to prevent this. Yet the gaps remain open, often because regulatory oversight is incomplete, incentives favor volume over rigor, and enforcement is weak across jurisdictions.

For every corporate buyer and project developer, the question is uncomfortable but necessary: how robust is the integrity of the system you are participating in? If double counting remains possible, then the "verified" label may be offering comfort rather than certainty.

The credibility of the entire voluntary market rests on closing these gaps—not eventually, but now.

CHINA WANTED ACCESS TO NVIDIA'S AI CHIPS. THE SPY SCANDAL MAY HAVE MADE THAT EVEN HARDER.

The controversy surrounding Jensen Huang has opened a new front in the technology battle between Washington and Beijing. And the consequences for China could be considerably more damaging than initially expected.

The allegations involving Huang and Alice Huang, a Singapore-based business executive suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence, have brought renewed attention to the movement of advanced American chips into China. Beijing denies the espionage allegations. They have not been independently established.

But Washington is responding with measures that extend well beyond the individuals involved.

Singapore-based Megaspeed has been blacklisted by the US Commerce Department. Additional restrictions now require export licenses for certain advanced AI chips shipped to several Southeast Asian countries, including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. These measures target routes that US officials believe could be used to divert restricted technology into China.

The commercial consequences are already becoming visible. Some Chinese customers have cancelled or delayed NVIDIA orders amid uncertainty over which products they will still be allowed to buy.

NVIDIA has also decided to stop selling even certain chips that had previously been permitted for export to China, including the H20 and H200.

For Beijing, this creates an uncomfortable situation. Chinese technology companies still want access to NVIDIA's processors and software. Yet the political climate in Washington is moving toward tighter scrutiny, not greater access.

There is another consequence. Every new restriction gives China's semiconductor industry another reason to accelerate its efforts to develop domestic alternatives. Companies such as Huawei are already working to close the gap, backed by substantial state support and a huge domestic market.

That will not happen overnight. NVIDIA retains significant advantages in chip performance, software and its developer ecosystem. Replacing that combination is a formidable undertaking.

But Washington should consider the longer-term consequences of its strategy. Restricting access to American technology can slow a competitor's progress in the short term. It can also give that competitor a powerful incentive to eliminate its dependence on American suppliers.

The immediate loser may be China's access to NVIDIA chips. The longer-term beneficiary could be China's own semiconductor industry.

And that is the strategic calculation Washington cannot afford to ignore.

Today, my 13 year-old son mentioned that the school talked about the #25November as the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. I was surprised that they made such an awareness at school but then I started pondering about it.

Violence is not only physical or verbal. It also lives quietly inside families and companies: by choices being made such as the job that goes to "him" by default, the innocent suggestions by the society to stay home and care for the children, the part-time or freelance years that turn into a small pension, etc. 

For example, when I first arrived in Italy, a Father in my son's catholic school responded that children should stay with their mothers when I suggested an after-school homework program after realising that school hours here do not permit women to work full-time. 

I wasn't even aware of gender discrimination until I left Singapore where I grew up. In Singapore and Norway, I never felt it: hiring, pay and promotion were about results. In Belgium, almost every woman I know works.

The numbers tell the same story:
▪️  Norway ranks 3rd of 148 countries in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2025. Italy ranks 85th.
▪️ In Italy, only 53.3% of women aged 15–64 are employed, against 71.1% of men (INPS, 2024 data).
▪️ Across the EU, women's pensions are 24.5% lower than men's. In Italy's private sector, women's old-age pensions are 46.2% lower.

I have had professional experiences in countries such as Singapore, Indonesia, Belgium, Norway and Italy and I am grateful that in every country I have lived in, I had male colleagues, leaders and clients who valued my work and me as a marketing professional. However, there are some women who aren't in the same situation. So this is about the merit of having a merit-based system in each company: what we can do should be judged by our knowledge, experience and results, not by the gender God gave each of us.

Yesterday at#WEAPN (Women Entrepreneurs and Professionals Network), we had a Business Talk about financial and investment planning for women, delivered in excellence byJulie Tedeschi who chose the date for this reason. I know too many women who paused their careers for a decade or two to raise children, worked part-time, or were passed over, and now face old age with too little. Financial freedom is protection.

Looking around WEAPN, I'm so proud to find that we have among us; engineers, lawyers, doctors, financial consultants, experts in many sectors. Most of us speak three or more languages and have worked in more than one country.

Now imagine if you have a daughter. Would you be happy with the path our society, especially in Italy, has set out for her? Leave your thoughts in the comment below. 👇

posts.text:
A flight-control system that could act on data from one sensor. Two fatal crashes. A fleet grounded worldwide.

This is a serious subject, and I want to treat it with respect. 346 people died in the two accidents: Lion Air Flight 610 in October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019. The 737 MAX was grounded worldwide in March 2019.

Investigators found that the flight-control software, called MCAS, could activate based on data from a single angle-of-attack sensor, even though the aircraft has two. A US House committee report said Boeing engineers had raised safety concerns about this during development. Indonesia's final report on the Lion Air crash described a chain of factors: design, maintenance and pilot response.

Different investigations emphasised different causes, and you should read them yourself. But some risk lessons are clear for anyone who runs projects:

1. A single point of failure belongs at the top of the risk register, with a plan.
If one input, one person or one supplier can stop everything, treat it as a high risk even if it is unlikely.
2. Pressure changes what teams accept as "safe enough."
Schedule and cost pressure are normal. The question is whether people feel free to raise concerns and whether those concerns reach the decision-maker.
3. A change to one part needs a fresh review of everything connected to it.
Small changes in a system can alter assumptions made earlier, in a different team.
4. Tell the people who use the system what it does.

Information that stays inside the project can still become a risk for the user.
Try this today: list the single points of failure in your project: one tool, one person, one supplier. Write a one-line fallback for each.

What is the single point of failure on your current project?

THE GLOBAL RACE FOR MINERALS AND AFRICA’S QUEST FOR INDUSTRIALISATION

By Johnbosco Novert Karungamye | Mining Engineer | Tanzania
  
The global race for critical minerals is not merely about securing raw materials. It is increasingly about securing industries, technologies, jobs, economic competitiveness and future prosperity.
  
First World Countries are strategically positioning themselves to secure mineral supply chains while strengthening domestic processing and manufacturing capabilities. The EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act (2024) targets domestic processing capacity equivalent to at least 40% of its annual consumption of strategic raw materials by 2030. Similarly, the United States’ Executive Order 14241 (2025) promotes domestic mineral extraction, processing, refining and manufacturing of mineral-derived products. Meanwhile, China and Indonesia accounted for over 75% of global growth in refined supplies of key energy minerals between 2023 and 2025 (IEA, 2026).

Africa’s industrial aspirations are founded on the same economic rationale.
According to the OECD's Regional review on Critical minerals in Africa, mining accounts for an average of 8.8% of GDP in mineral-rich African countries and generates more than half of their export revenues. In Tanzania, for instance, the mining sector accounted for 10.3% of national GDP and generated approximately 52.6% of total export earnings in 2025, having attracted USD 442.2 million in foreign direct investment (FDI) in 2024. Yet, the OECD reports that, 96% of Africa’s critical mineral exports are in raw or semi-processed form, with unprocessed minerals accounting for 24% and semi-processed minerals for 72%, reflecting the continent’s considerable untapped potential for deeper participation in higher-value downstream activities.
  
Africa’s pursuit of domestic mineral value addition is, therefore, an economically justified development pathway towards industrial expansion, employment creation, technology acquisition, skills development, local enterprise participation, increased foreign exchange earnings and economic diversification. This aspiration is reflected in Africa’s Green Minerals Strategy and Tanzania’s Development Vision 2050.
  
However, successful mineral-based industrialization must be pursued with economic and technical realism. It requires commercially viable projects, competitive energy and infrastructure, appropriate technologies, skilled human capital, predictable regulatory frameworks and strategic investment partnerships.
  
Global mineral supply security and Africa’s industrialization should not be competing objectives, but complementary ambitions. The opportunity, therefore, is not to choose between global mineral supply security and Africa's industrialization, but to design investment partnerships that deliver both.

This stunning 1917 paining Wayang Golek (Indonesian Puppet Theatre) I was bidding on just sold inInvaluable auction. How much do you think it went for?

The author is a Duch women,Cornelie Josephine Wilhelmina Slager (1883-1927).

I am going to quote the auction description because it matters. I found this painting of museum quality, and yet it's the first time I saw her name.

"In 1916, Slager married Louis van Dam, an engineer whose position as a director of the National Railways took him to the Dutch East Indies (present-day Indonesia), where he was involved in the construction of railway infrastructure. Accompanying her husband to the archipelago, Slager encountered a profoundly different natural and cultural environment, whose distinctive visual traditions and luxuriant landscapes became an important source of artistic inspiration.

The present painting is particularly significant within Slager's relatively small surviving oeuvre. Primarily a watercolourist, Slager produced comparatively few oils, a circumstance attributable in part to the limited availability of suitable materials beyond Java. The work also relates directly to her documented exhibition activity in the Dutch East Indies. Contemporary press accounts record that Slager exhibited several paintings at the local Kunstkring (Art Circle) in 1918, where her depictions of wayang golek - traditional wooden puppets used in Javanese performance - were singled out for their 'witty in conception and tasteful in color.' The present composition, with its carefully considered arrangement and measured chromatic relationships, demonstrates her sensitivity to the formal and cultural character of this enduring theatrical tradition.

Of considerable historical and artistic interest, the painting represents a rare and substantial example of Slager's work produced during her time in the Dutch East Indies. Its scale is particularly noteworthy within an oeuvre more commonly associated with smaller, intimate watercolours. Slager's relative obscurity within the history of Dutch art reflects not only her premature death at the age of 43, but also the broader historical marginalisation of women artists, whose contributions have frequently received less scholarly and institutional attention than those of their male contemporaries. The present work offers an important opportunity to reassess her artistic achievement within the wider context of Dutch colonial-era painting and the intercultural encounters that informed her practice."

It sold for $5,500 AUD. I wonder if her painting would have sold for a higher price if she had been a man.

I didn't get it, of course (I didn't have much hope, honestly, but sometimes I do get incredible bargain, like these 2 Middle Eastern rope slung chairs and a table... $100! Yes, one hundred dollars. I am collecting hand made items like this because they have a soul, and because I firmly believe they will be very valuable in future when people will stop making them.)

How are field survey measurements transformed into information that supports mining operations? This was one of the questions I explored firsthand during my internship at PT Mineral Alam Abadi’s Obi site.

From July to September 2026, I joined the Survey Department as a Mine Survey Engineer Intern at an open-pit nickel mine on Obi Island, North Maluku, Indonesia. This experience allowed me to apply my knowledge of Geodesy and Geomatics while gaining an understanding of the practical challenges of mine surveying.

Under the survey team’s guidance, I participated in topographic surveys using GNSS RTK and Total Station, as well as aerial mapping with RTK-enabled drones. I also assisted with staking out drill holes, mining boundaries, crest and toe positions, and road alignments, alongside elevation checks against design references, control point surveys, and geotechnical monitoring.

For data processing, I used Microsoft Excel, GEOVIA Surpac, Agisoft Metashape, Global Mapper, and QGIS to check coordinates, process aerial imagery, build Digital Terrain Models (DTMs), calculate cut-and-fill volumes, and produce contours and topographic maps. These tasks helped me understand how field data quality affects the information delivered to operational teams.

One memorable experience was our team’s topographic mapping project at P16, Pit Anyer. Using 835 detail points, 2 benchmarks, and 5 Ground Control Points, we produced a terrain model, a topographic map with 2-meter contour intervals, and a technical report evaluating data quality and survey limitations.

Beyond technical skills, I learned to adapt to field conditions, communicate within a team, and follow workplace safety procedures. This experience reinforced the importance of planning, attention to detail, and coordination at every stage of survey work.

Thank you to PT Mineral Alam Abadi and the entire Survey Department at the Obi site for this valuable learning opportunity. Special thanks to Pak Rahmat Yudhistira, Pak Sonna Budhiwangsa Legian, and Pak Rai Akbar Jawadi for their guidance, technical insights, and support throughout my internship. I am also grateful to my fellow interns for their teamwork and companionship throughout this experience.

Protests at BYD’s US$1 billion EV plant in Subang, West Java, highlight growing friction between Indonesia’s push for high-tech foreign investment and local communities' demands for immediate jobs.

• The Hiring Dispute: Local demonstrators (FMSB) claim Subang residents make up under 20% of the plant's staff and are demanding a mandatory 70% local hiring quota, transparent recruitment, and vocational training. BYD countered that out of nearly 6,000 employees, 90% are Indonesian—with 80% from West Java and roughly 1,300 workers (30% of the West Java share) from Subang—while reiterating a long-term goal to hire up to 20,000 locals.
• Skills Gap vs. Unemployment: High automation in EV manufacturing requires specialized experience that many local residents lack due to delayed vocational training programs. Meanwhile, West Java’s 6.67% unemployment rate (well above the 4.75% national average) fuels local fears of being left behind by capital-intensive projects.

• Investor Security: Repeated disruptions from mass organizations (ormas) from construction into operations have led BYD to request stronger state protection, raising concerns among economists that unrest could threaten broader foreign investment deals with China.

• Government Mediation: West Java Governor Dedi Mulyadi and central officials are intervening to curb disruptive blockades while pushing manufacturers to speed up local skills transfer and hiring commitments.

Today, my 13 year-old son mentioned that the school talked about the #25November as the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. I was surprised that they made such an awareness at school but then I started pondering about it.

Violence is not only physical or verbal. It also lives quietly inside families and companies: by choices being made such as the job that goes to "him" by default, the innocent suggestions by the society to stay home and care for the children, the part-time or freelance years that turn into a small pension, etc. 

For example, when I first arrived in Italy, a Father in my son's catholic school responded that children should stay with their mothers when I suggested an after-school homework program after realising that school hours here do not permit women to work full-time. 

I wasn't even aware of gender discrimination until I left Singapore where I grew up. In Singapore and Norway, I never felt it: hiring, pay and promotion were about results. In Belgium, almost every woman I know works.

The numbers tell the same story:
▪️  Norway ranks 3rd of 148 countries in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2025. Italy ranks 85th.
▪️ In Italy, only 53.3% of women aged 15–64 are employed, against 71.1% of men (INPS, 2024 data).
▪️ Across the EU, women's pensions are 24.5% lower than men's. In Italy's private sector, women's old-age pensions are 46.2% lower.

I have had professional experiences in countries such as Singapore, Indonesia, Belgium, Norway and Italy and I am grateful that in every country I have lived in, I had male colleagues, leaders and clients who valued my work and me as a marketing professional. However, there are some women who aren't in the same situation. So this is about the merit of having a merit-based system in each company: what we can do should be judged by our knowledge, experience and results, not by the gender God gave each of us.

Yesterday at#WEAPN (Women Entrepreneurs and Professionals Network), we had a Business Talk about financial and investment planning for women, delivered in excellence byJulie Tedeschi who chose the date for this reason. I know too many women who paused their careers for a decade or two to raise children, worked part-time, or were passed over, and now face old age with too little. Financial freedom is protection.

Looking around WEAPN, I'm so proud to find that we have among us; engineers, lawyers, doctors, financial consultants, experts in many sectors. Most of us speak three or more languages and have worked in more than one country.

Now imagine if you have a daughter. Would you be happy with the path our society, especially in Italy, has set out for her? Leave your thoughts in the comment below. 👇

Last Tuesday was a busy day for us in Jakarta. In the morning, we hosted a LIHAthon, guiding Talent Acquisition teams on how to use LinkedIn Hiring Assistant—not just to automate repetitive candidate search tasks, but to hire for skills rather than just job titles. Then in the evening, we hosted aCHRO x CFO dinner on the future of talent.

There's one question from last week's events that stayed with me:'What if we invest in our people and they leave?' At the same time there was a quiet apprehension about the next generation taking over...all while stressing over succession planning. Funny paradox: we worry about them stepping up, and we worry about having no one ready to step up. So we stand still. Then wrap it all under cost optimization. 

The data offers a helpful perspective here. Our 2026 Talent Velocity Advantage Report shows thatcompanies treating learning as a core investment outperform peers in retention and profitability confidence. That mindset shift feels especially relevant in Indonesia. Taking AI skills as an example, the country leads globally in relative AI talent growth, yet AI remains the hardest skill for employers to find (something I hear in my everyday conversations with HR leaders too!) 

It makes me wonder: is it a talent shortage, a visibility gap, or an execution gap in how we actually use those skills? If as a company we don’t know the skills we have versus the skills we need or even how to deploy them...how do we then build? And without a clear plan on what to build, how do we justify the budget?

Big questions with plenty of perspectives, and a conversation worth continuing! Our team will be hosting a webinar on Learning on December 11—stay tuned!

Freelancers vs remote hiring: which one actually takes work off your plate?

When a Singapore SME team is stretched, the default reaction is to hire a freelancer or sign a small agency retainer.

That works for a one-off campaign or a website rebuild. It breaks down when the work is daily and operational: answering customer enquiries, reconciling invoices, updating product listings, or keeping marketing schedules on track.

Freelancers split their week across five or six clients. Every time your priorities shift, you spend hours re-briefing someone who does not sit inside your workflows.

A dedicated remote employee solves a different problem. They work for your business alone, inside your Slack, your CRM, and your SOPs.

You keep full control over what drives revenue:

- Setting daily priorities and KPIs
- Training them on your internal processes
- Reviewing output and developing their skills over time

Redox handles the side that usually slows cross-border hiring down: sourcing and screening candidates, local Indonesian employment contracts, monthly payroll, statutory requirements, and ongoing AI enablement, without your company needing to open a foreign entity.

Why Indonesia? Jakarta is one hour behind Singapore and Bali shares your time zone, so your hire is online during your working day, not overnight. And there is a deep pool of experienced professionals in marketing, admin, finance, and digital roles who already work with regional teams.

A visa and an invitation are only the start.

This week our team was at the Indonesia Poland Business Forum in Warsaw, hosted by the Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia. The topic: connecting Polish businesses with skilled workers from Indonesia.

The questions in the room weren't about recruitment. They were about what happens after:

→ What happens to workers once they land in Poland?
→ Why do some candidates never arrive?
→ Why are deportation rates so high?
→ Why do many decide not to stay?

From what we see every day, most of these stories don't start with bad intentions. They start with a missed deadline, an unread letter from the office, or a residence card application filed too late.

For employers, this means retention starts on day one:

1. Start the residence card process before the visa expires
2. Keep contracts and notifications on time
3. Make sure someone helps your people understand letters from the office
4. Think about family and relocation, not just the job

You invest in hiring. Legalisation is what protects that investment.

We help companies handle legalisation for their foreign teams end-to-end - from the MOS application to the card in hand.

Thank you to the Embassy of Indonesia in Warsaw for bringing these conversations to the table.

Instead, Gerstner kept the organization whole and made a contrarian bet: enterprises didn’t want another catalog of boxes—they needed an integrator to solve end-to-end business problems. Within justfew years, he swung the company from billions loss to a $$5.4B profit, scaled a strong services engine, and proved the thesis behind his famous memoir, Who Says Elephants Can’t Dance?

In one of the world’s most dynamic, mobile-first, and rapidly digitizing regions, enterprises are aggressively investing in Digital Transformation, Hybrid Cloud, AI, and Next-Gen Networking. Yet across boardrooms from Marina Bay to Jakarta, Bangkok, and Kuala Lumpur, a clear reality is emerging: technology alone does not guarantee transformation.

Procuring cutting-edge compute, foundational AI models, and modern network fabric is only the starting line. Without a cohesive services layer to orchestrate them across diverse regional footprints, organizations risk creating fragmented silos instead of scalable business outcomes.

High-impact services are what turn architectural ambition into measurable ASEAN market leadership:

Hybrid Cloud & Next-Gen Networking: Operating across Southeast Asia means navigating varying data residency laws, multi-market latency, and complex legacy estates. Advisory and managed services deliver seamless workload placement, zero-trust security, and deterministic connectivity from the edge to the core.

Operationalizing Sovereign & Enterprise AI: Moving AI from isolated pilots to production requires clean data pipelines, strict regulatory governance, and localized MLOps. Services bridge the gap between raw AI infrastructure and trusted, repeatable ROI.

End-to-End Digital Transformation: True modernization ties IT architecture directly to P&L impact—accelerating cross-border expansion, optimizing operational costs, and building digital resilience.

A CTO’s Perspective: Regional Scale Needs Choreography From a CTO vantage point in Southeast Asia, the hardest challenge is never selecting a point product; it is orchestrating an agile, compliant ecosystem across multiple markets at varying stages of digital maturity. A stack of AI, cloud, and network tools without a unified services strategy is like having a world-class orchestra without a conductor. As technology leaders, our mandate is not merely to deploy infrastructure—it is to engineer business agility. Strategic services provide the architectural blueprints, integration muscle, and operational discipline required to make complex environments perform as one unified engine.

Technology is the foundation, but purposeful services are what make the enterprise move. When aligned with clear business outcomes, services aren't an implementation afterthought—they are the catalyst that teaches the elephant how to dance.

Legacy Java 8 code? AI can help you modernize it to Java 21, if you do it right.

Nobody enjoys migrating old code. But AI is surprisingly good at the repetitive parts, as long as you stay in control. This is the approach I use.

**1️⃣ Build a safety net first**

No tests, no refactor. If coverage is thin, ask AI to generate characterization tests that lock in the current behavior. Then review them. They're your proof that nothing broke.

**2️⃣ Refactor in small batches**

One class or one pattern at a time. Never "migrate the whole project" in one prompt.

**3️⃣ Let AI handle the mechanical upgrades**

```java
// Before
if (o instanceof Order) {
  Order x = (Order) o;
  return x.getId();
}

// After
if (o instanceof Order x) {
  return x.id();
}
```

Good candidates:
• Pattern matching for instanceof and switch
• Records instead of boilerplate DTOs
• Text blocks, `var`, and stream cleanups
• `javax.*` to `jakarta.*` for Spring Boot 3
• Replacing deprecated APIs

**4️⃣ Use it to break up the monolith (carefully)**

AI is great for mapping dependencies: "Which classes use the billing package?" or "Propose module boundaries for this code." Treat the answer as a starting point for discussion, not a design.

**5️⃣ Review every diff, run the build, run the tests**

```
Refactor this class to Java 21 features.
Keep behavior identical. Don't change public
method signatures. List every change you made.
```

**⚠️ Watch out for**
• Subtle behavior changes (null handling, equality, ordering)
• Hallucinated APIs or wrong library versions
• Records replacing classes that JPA entities or serializers rely on
• Huge diffs nobody can review
• Pasting proprietary code into unapproved tools

**💡 Tips**
• Use OpenRewrite for deterministic, large-scale migrations, and AI for the judgment calls around them
• Commit after every step so you can roll back easily
• Let CI be the referee

AI makes the boring part faster. The discipline is still yours.

I have been building a multi-page website for Greenfield Academy with React and Vite, and this week was about the details that make a site feel finished.

Here is what I worked on:
1. Set up a consistent brand colour palette across every page.
2. Chose Playfair Display for headings and Plus Jakarta Sans for body text, then used browser DevTools to confirm the fonts were actually rendering and not falling back to defaults.
3. Replaced emojis and default arrows with lucide-react icons in the header, homepage and footer, which made the whole interface look cleaner and more professional.
4. Tracked down image loading problems so every visual displays properly.

What I learned: 
Small things like fonts, icons and images decide whether a site looks like a tutorial or like a real product. Checking that something works in the browser, and not just assuming it does, saves a lot of time.
I am still refining it, and I will share the live version soon.
